newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan says handback of Chinese hijackers imminent.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan says handback of Chinese hijackers imminent.

text.p: Taipei said on Tuesday that two mainland hijackers who commandeered airliners to Taiwan would be returned soon to rival China, reciprocating Beijing's May repatriation of a Taiwanese hijacker.

"We plan to send a letter to our (Beijing) counterpart in a day or two, informing them that we will soon repatriate the two mainland hijackers," Reed You, legal services director of Taiwan's Straits Exchange Foundation, said.

The semi-official foundation and Beijing's Association for Relations Across the Taiwan Strait handle bilateral contacts in the absence of official communications between Beijing and Taiwan, estranged since a 1949 civil war split.

Chang King-yuh, Taiwan's top mainland policymaker, has said his cabinet-level Mainland Affairs Council agreed to consider repatriating Han Fengying and Huang Shugang, who have served out four-year prison terms for air piracy.
Han and Huang, who may face new trials in China on capital air piracy charges, are in detention at a special centre for illegal aliens from the mainland.
The foundation's You said the only outstanding issue was the mechanics of the repatriation.
"We need to know who they will send to fetch the two hijackers," You said.
Taiwan holds 16 mainlanders, who hijacked 12 mainland planes to Taiwan in 1993-1994 before China tightened airport security.

In May, Beijing returned Taiwanese air pirate Liu Shan-chung in the first cross-strait hijacker repatriation despite its own two-year-old freeze on talks with Taiwan and the absence of a formal repatriation pact.

Taiwan and China, which have had no formal links since civil war split them in 1949, reached unofficial consensus on hijacker repatriation in 1995 but failed to sign the accord because of subsequent political frictions.
Beijing froze semi-official talks in June 1995 in protest against a landmark private visit to the United States by Taiwan President Lee Teng-hui, whom it accused of seeking Taiwan's independence.
Beijing has stonewalled Taipei's calls to resume the talks, saying dialogue was impossible before Taiwan agreed to stop engaging in what China called "splittist" activities.

Speculation has mounted in recent weeks that Britain's July 1 handover of Hong Kong to China would offer a chance for renewed contacts between the two negotiating bodies, whose leaders are both expected to attend.
Taiwan officials have said such contacts would be welcome but cautioned that significant negotiations were not planned and would require more formal preparations.
